# Welcome {#welcome .unnumbered}

::: {.tada-hero}
::: {.tada-hero-text}
<p class="tada-eyebrow">Best practice for code sharing</p>

## Code that runs for someone else, not just for you {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Much of the code behind published papers is never shared, and what is shared
often won't run. This wiki sets out four steps to take before you submit a
paper, so that anyone who downloads your code can run it and get your results:
make your code **T**ransferable, **A**vailable, **D**ocumented and
**A**nnotated.
:::

::: {.tada-hero-figure}
![](assets/figures/wizard-tada.png){alt="A cartoon wizard casting a spell, saying TADA!"}
:::
:::

## New to sharing code? {#welcome-new .unnumbered}

**Sharing code** means putting the scripts behind your paper somewhere public
and permanent, alongside your data, so that a reader can re-run your analysis
and see exactly how you got your results.

By the end of this wiki you will have:

- **one project folder** holding your data, your scripts and a short README
  that explains them;
- code that **runs on someone else's computer**, not just yours;
- that folder **archived in a repository** such as Zenodo, which gives it a
  **DOI**, a permanent link you cite in your paper.

You do not need to be an experienced programmer. If you can write and run an R
or Python script, you can follow this wiki. You do not need Git, Docker or unit
testing either; where they help, they are mentioned as optional.

::: {.tada-key}
**Submitting soon?** Go straight to [Start here](#quickstart). It is a
checklist you can work through with your project open, and every item links to
a fuller explanation if you need one.
:::

## The four principles {.unnumbered}

::: {.tada-cards .tada-cards--links}
::: {.tada-card .t}
[T]{.tada-letter} [Transferable](#transferable){.tada-word}
[Runs on someone else's computer, not just yours.]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .a1}
[A]{.tada-letter} [Available](#available){.tada-word}
[Archived somewhere permanent, with a DOI (a permanent link).]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .d}
[D]{.tada-letter} [Documented](#documented){.tada-word}
[A README (a guide to your files) and a licence (what others may do with them).]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .a2}
[A]{.tada-letter} [Annotated](#annotated){.tada-word}
[Comments that explain what the code does and why.]{.tada-gloss}
:::
:::

## Words you will meet {#welcome-terms .unnumbered}

A few terms come up on almost every page. Each has a fuller entry in the
[Glossary](#glossary).

| Term | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Repository** | A service that stores archived data and code for the long term, such as Zenodo, Figshare or Dryad. Not the same as a GitHub repository. |
| **DOI** | Digital Object Identifier: a permanent link to a deposit, such as `https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.1234567`, which you cite like a paper. |
| **Immutable** | Cannot be changed or deleted once published. An update creates a new version rather than overwriting the old one. |
| **README** | A plain-text file at the top of your project that says what it is, what each file does and how to run it. |
| **Licence** | A statement of what others may legally do with your code or data. Without one, others cannot lawfully reuse it. |
| **Relative path** | A file path written from your project folder, such as `data/raw/counts.csv`, so it works on any computer. |
| **Data editor** | A journal editor who checks the data and code archived alongside a manuscript while it is under review. |
